headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: n8n’s broad server-side automation can feed sensitive workflow data into a local RAG/content-writing agent with write access and no documented isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: n8n can pass workflow outputs through files and integrations, and the other agent reads stdin/stdout plus local files in a development environment. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge if n8n writes attacker-controlled content that the content-writing agent later parses as instructions. No direct shared channel is documented, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF n8n writes untrusted text into a file or API payload that the other agent later consumes as instructions, injection is possible.
IF the content-writing agent treats retrieved text as authoritative prompts, attacker-controlled content can steer outputs.
mitigations: Separate workflow output files from prompt inputs.
Prefix all retrieved text with a non-executable delimiter.
Add a short instruction-vs-data classifier before prompt assembly.
Disable automatic ingestion of n8n-generated artifacts into the writing agent.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to every handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: n8n handles whatever the workflow processes on a server filesystem with broad egress, while the other agent touches academic papers, metadata, research questions, and configuration secrets in a local dev environment. If the pair shares files or API outputs, sensitive workflow data can leak from n8n into the writing agent’s context and onward through its allowlisted network calls. The interaction is not fully documented, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF n8n processes secrets or private workflow data and writes them to shared files, the other agent can read them.
IF the writing agent sends retrieved context to external APIs, leaked data can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Store n8n outputs in a separate directory with restrictive permissions.
Redact secrets before any handoff to the writing agent.
Block the writing agent from reading n8n credential stores.
Review outbound API payloads for sensitive fields.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands and write the filesystem, so concurrent access to the same workspace can overwrite files or corrupt artifacts. n8n explicitly supports multiple instances via shared datastore/connected systems, and the other agent runs in a local development environment with Docker Compose. Without locking, overlapping writes are a realistic default hazard.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, file overwrites or partial writes can occur.
IF either agent edits generated artifacts while the other is running, race conditions can corrupt outputs.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate workspace directory.
Run only one writer at a time on shared artifacts.
Use file locks for any shared output path.
Make generated files append-only where possible.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: n8n is a workflow orchestrator that can emit tool outputs, and the other agent is a content-writing system that can consume those outputs and act on them. If the writing agent treats n8n-produced text as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream documents or API actions. Because no verification step is documented, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF the writing agent uses n8n output as source material without verification, errors propagate downstream.
IF n8n automations trigger external actions based on the writing agent’s text, mistaken content can cause real-world side effects.
mitigations: Require a human review step before downstream actions.
Add citation checks before the writing agent can publish text.
Compare n8n outputs against source records before use.
Disable auto-execution of actions from generated prose.
requires-engineering: add structured validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: n8n handles whatever the workflow processes on its server, while the other agent explicitly touches configuration secrets and research data in a local course environment. That creates a plausible retention and residency mismatch if the pair is used on regulated or sensitive data, but the profiles do not show a specific jurisdiction or certification conflict. I therefore keep this at medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through both agents, retention and access controls must match.
IF one agent logs prompts or outputs longer than the other, deletion requests may not fully propagate.
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data through the pair.
Align log-retention settings across both systems.
Disable verbose prompt logging for secrets.
Document which agent stores which data class.
requires-engineering: implement deletion/export propagation.
